cells.tense: You're in it right now, looking after something, and you know that's what you're doing.
cells.ask: Give what's growing one more day of room than it needs, and say out loud one thing you saw it do.
cells.core:
There's something in front of you that needs looking after, and you're the one who does it. You feed it, you wait on it, you leave it alone when leaving it alone is the right move — and the thing you're looking after keeps growing because of it. That's not luck. You've been reading what it needs and giving that, and nothing else, and it's landing. You catch the moment it's thirsty before it droops, and you don't rush the rest.

Steady direction comes out of feeling here, not out of forcing. Say what you saw it do this week, out loud, once — to whoever's around or to the wall — and the next right move shows up on its own. The proof that it was you doing it is already in the growing.
cells.sheetLine: You're looking after it, and it's growing.
cells.verb: Two streams meeting and deciding to flow as one
cells.place: Where what is growing gets looked after

cells.tense: You're standing in a day that hasn't arrived yet, braced, working to make it come out right.
cells.ask: Put down one thing you're doing for it that nobody asked for — one day without it — and see what it does on its own.
cells.core:
Something's growing near you and you're doing the growing for it. You watch it, you water it, you check it, and the checking turned into a job. Somewhere in there the gripping started feeling like love, and the plant or the person or the project — whatever it is — started getting your hands instead of your attention. The faster you work, the less you feel like you're helping.

Care that doesn't tire you out is the way back. Holding space without squeezing it, tending without doing the part that belongs to the thing itself. Put one thing down for a day and watch what stands. What stays up while your hands are off it is what was yours to hold in the first place.

cells.tense: You're beside something that needs looking after, and the looking-after has gone quiet in you.
cells.ask: Sit with one thing you're looking after for five minutes without deciding anything, and write one plain sentence about what you noticed.
cells.core:
There's something in front of you that needs someone, and the someone isn't showing up in you the way it used to. It's not that you don't care — it's that looking after it stopped feeling like looking after it, and the quiet has gone further than you meant it to. The thing is still growing. You're just not the one in the room with it right now. Nearby, this looks like hands on it in the morning, an eye on it at night, and nothing forced in between.

Say one plain thing you know about it, without working out what it means or what to do next. You already take things in; you just stopped saying them. The first sentence is the way back, and the second one comes easier.

cells.tense: You're looking after it right now, and talking about it like it happens by itself.
cells.ask: Say one sentence out loud that names the shape you're giving what's growing, and hear your own voice say it.
cells.core:
Something's growing here and it has a shape, and you're the one who's been giving it that shape. The room, the light, the timing, the words, what you let in and what you keep out — none of it happened by itself, and none of it is a stranger's doing either. Yet the telling of it comes out like the thing chose its own shape, and you're the only one who hasn't been let in on it.

What you practice carries itself when you stop forcing it. Name the shape as yours, out loud, once. What it gives back is the work getting lighter, because the one doing it is finally in the room.
cells.sheetLine: You're giving it its shape. Say so.

attempts.check: The draft risked claiming the person picks who to grow alongside, which the record does not establish — a reader in a group home or an unavoidable family could say that's not true, so every cell now stays on tending rather than on choosing who is near. The asks are steps about a plant, a photo, a written sheet, or a named truth, so they still teach something if the read is wrong. The watched line ('a watched seed doesn't') served the writer's love of shape more than the reader, and is cut. Some sentences are set to run only in this case, so their main work is here and not only for whoever writes next.
